title: Composition vs Inheritance
summary: Has-a vs is-a, and why "favor composition over inheritance" became standard advice — delegation, coupling, and refactoring a rigid hierarchy into a flexible one.

slides.markdown:
**Composition** builds a class out of other objects it holds a reference to — has-a — and forwards work to them, instead of inheriting their code directly — is-a. Both are legitimate reuse strategies, but composition avoids the tight coupling and fragility that deep inheritance hierarchies accumulate.

This topic covers the has-a/is-a test, why "favor composition" became default advice, and how to refactor a rigid inheritance hierarchy into a composed, swappable design.

slides.sectionTitle: Has-a vs is-a: the test for which relationship you actually have
slides.markdown:
**Is-a** justifies inheritance: a `Car` is a `Vehicle`, so extending it is honest. **Has-a** justifies composition: a `Car` has an `Engine` — it doesn't make sense to say "a Car is an Engine," but it absolutely holds one and delegates `start()` to it.

The test in practice: try finishing the sentence "a `X` is a `Y`" out loud. If it sounds natural and holds for every instance — every `Car` really is a `Vehicle`, always — inheritance fits. If it sounds forced, or only sometimes true ("a `Car` is an `Engine`"? no), you actually have a has-a relationship, and composition is the honest model.

Getting this test wrong is the single most common root cause of the problems later slides describe — fragile hierarchies almost always started from a has-a relationship modeled as is-a because it was convenient at the time.

slides.sectionTitle: "Favor composition over inheritance" — where that advice comes from
slides.markdown:
This phrase, popularized by the *Design Patterns* ("Gang of Four") book, isn't "never use inheritance" — it's a default preference, for concrete reasons observed across real codebases. Inheritance couples a subclass to its base class's implementation details, not just its public contract (the fragile base class problem from the Inheritance topic); composition couples a class only to the interface of the object it holds.

Inheritance is also fixed at compile time — a `Car`'s relationship to `Vehicle` can't change while the program runs. Composition can be swapped at runtime — a `Car` holding an `Engine` reference can be handed a different `Engine` implementation on the fly, which inheritance structurally cannot do.

The advice's actual shape: use inheritance for genuine, stable is-a relationships; reach for composition by default everywhere else, especially when you're tempted to inherit purely to reuse behavior.

slides.sectionTitle: Delegation: forwarding calls to a composed object
slides.markdown:
**Delegation** is how composition actually reuses behavior: instead of inheriting a method, a class holds a reference to another object and forwards the call to it. `Car.start()` doesn't reimplement engine-starting logic — it calls `this.engine.start()`, letting the held `Engine` object do the real work.

From the outside, `car.start()` looks just like it would with inheritance — one method call, one apparent action. The difference is entirely structural: with inheritance, `start()`'s code is copied into `Car`'s own method table via the class hierarchy; with delegation, `Car` owns none of that code, it just knows who to ask.

That structural difference is what buys flexibility — swap `this.engine` for a different `Engine` implementation (electric instead of combustion) at construction time or even later, and `car.start()` now does something entirely different with zero changes to `Car` itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the same feature modeled via inheritance vs composition, side by side
slides.markdown:
Modeling "a Car that can start": the inheritance version has `Car extends Engine` — which already reads wrong, since a Car isn't a kind of Engine — baking one specific engine's `start()` logic permanently into `Car`. The composition version has `Car` holding a field `Engine engine`, with `Car.start()` calling `engine.start()`.

Swapping engine types shows the practical gap: the inheritance version needs a new subclass (`ElectricCar extends ElectricEngine`) and can't change which engine a given `Car` instance uses after construction. The composition version just constructs `Car` with a different `Engine` object — same `Car` class, different behavior, decided at runtime.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: inheritance vs composition — reuse, coupling, runtime flexibility
slides.markdown:
The trade-offs, side by side, framed around what actually breaks in practice:

| | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship modeled | is-a | has-a |
| Coupling | Tight — subclass depends on base class internals, not just its public API | Loose — depends only on the held object's interface |
| Flexibility | Fixed at compile time; can't change a class's parent at runtime | Can swap the composed object at runtime |
| Reuse mechanism | Automatic (inherited methods) | Explicit (delegation, must be written) |
| Risk as it grows | Fragile base class, deep hierarchies get hard to reason about | More boilerplate (forwarding methods), but each piece stays isolated |

**How to decide:** default to composition; reach for inheritance only when the is-a relationship is genuine, stable, and you're confident the base class's behavior won't need to change underneath existing subclasses.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: refactoring an inheritance hierarchy into a composed strategy
Pitfall: deep inheritance chains that are impossible to reason about
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Each subclass only adds a small, understandable amount on top of its parent, so a five- or six-level hierarchy is still manageable."

**Why it's wrong:** understanding what a leaf class actually does requires holding the *entire chain* in your head at once — every override, every `super` call, every field from every ancestor — because behavior at the bottom can depend on any of it. A bug in a five-level-deep subclass might trace back to an assumption baked into the second level, discovered only by reading all five files in sequence.

**Correct model:** treat hierarchy depth as a cost that compounds, not a free way to organize code — two or three levels is usually the practical ceiling before "favor composition" should kick in. If you find yourself creating a subclass just to override one small piece of behavior, that's usually a signal the varying piece should be extracted into a composed, swappable object instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Where the Strategy pattern replaces a hierarchy of behavior subclasses
slides.markdown:
The refactor from the earlier code slide has a name: the **Strategy pattern** — extract a piece of varying behavior into its own interface, implement each variant as a small class, and have the main class hold and delegate to whichever implementation it's given. It's the standard, named answer to "I have a hierarchy that only exists to vary one behavior."

Recognize the smell that calls for it: a base class with one method that every subclass overrides differently, and nothing else distinguishing the subclasses — that's not really an inheritance hierarchy, it's one behavior with several implementations wearing a hierarchy's clothing.

This is a specific, common instance of the broader composition-over-inheritance advice — worth naming by pattern name in an interview, since "I'd apply Strategy here" signals you recognize the shape of the problem, not just the general principle.
